title: Design a URL Shortener (TinyURL)
tagline: Turn long links into short ones and redirect billions of clicks, reliably.

statement.prompt: Design a service like TinyURL or bit.ly. A user pastes a long link and gets back a short one. Anyone who opens the short link is sent to the original page.
context: You are in a 45-minute system design interview. The interviewer gave you only the sentence above, on purpose. Part of the job is finding out what they actually want.
The service is public: anyone on the internet can create and open links.
Think of a product that already exists. A link like `https://tiny.example/aZ3k9Qp` should open `https://www.example.com/blog/2024/a-very-long-article-title?utm_source=newsletter&ref=42`.
given: About **100 million** new short links are created every month.
Reading is far more common than writing: roughly **100 redirects for every link created**.
Links are kept for **5 years** unless the owner sets an earlier expiry.
An average stored record (short code, long URL, dates, owner) is about **500 bytes**.

expectations.title: Drive the conversation
expectations.body: Ask questions before drawing anything. State your assumptions out loud so they can be corrected early.

expectations.title: Use numbers
expectations.body: Turn the givens into requests per second, storage and bandwidth. Every later choice should point back to one of these numbers.

expectations.title: Start simple, then evolve
expectations.body: Get a working client, server and database on the board first. Add caches, sharding and queues only when a number or a requirement asks for them.

expectations.title: Go deep on the hard parts
expectations.body: For this problem the hard parts are generating unique short codes, serving very fast reads and scaling the data store.

expectations.title: Name the trade-offs
expectations.body: Say what you chose, what you gave up, and what would make you change your mind.

expectations.title: Think about failure
expectations.body: Point out single points of failure and say what happens when a node, a cache or a whole zone goes down.

scope_in: Creating a short link from a long URL
Redirecting a short link to the original URL
Scaling reads and storage, keeping the service available
scope_out: Detailed analytics dashboards (a click count is fine)
Billing, abuse review tooling and spam detection internals
great: Explains why a **302** redirect can be better than a **301**.
Compares at least three ways to make short codes and says why one wins.
Chooses a shard key from the access pattern, not from habit.
Handles a cache that goes down without taking the database down with it.

concepts.def: Write a number using 62 symbols (a-z, A-Z, 0-9). 7 characters give about 3.5 trillion codes.
301 is permanent and cached by browsers (less load, no click counting). 302 is temporary, so every click reaches you.
The app checks the cache, and on a miss reads the database and stores the result in the cache.
Place keys and nodes on a ring so adding a shard moves only a small share of keys.
Many more reads than writes (here 100 to 1), so optimise the read path first.

numbers: ~6 billion records x 500 B = about **3 TB** in 5 years

takeaways: Clarify first: **create, redirect, custom alias, expiry**.
Numbers: **40 writes/s, 4,000 reads/s, 3 TB** — a read-heavy problem.
Generate codes from **counter ranges + base62**, scrambled so they are not guessable.
Serve reads with **cache-aside + LRU**; use **302** to keep control.
Scale with **sharding by hash(code)** and **replicas across zones**.

tradeoffs.gain: Clicks, expiry and edits keep working
Easy to scale, fast by key

tradeoffs.cost: A new link may take a moment to appear everywhere

extensions: Click analytics pipeline through a queue
Abuse and malware scanning on creation

steps.title: What should the system do?
steps.prompt: Before drawing anything, you ask the interviewer what the system must do. Which of these belong in the **core** scope for a 45-minute design? Select all that apply.
steps.hint: Ask: what is the smallest product that is still a URL shortener? Then ask what would be nice to have.

options.text: Create a short URL from a long URL
options.why: This is the whole point of the product.

options.text: Redirect a short URL to the original long URL
options.why: The other half of the product, and the one used most.

options.text: Optional custom alias, such as tiny.example/my-sale
options.why: Common in real products. It changes how you store and check codes, so confirm it early.

options.text: Links can expire after a date set by the creator
options.why: Expiry affects storage cleanup and the redirect status code, so it belongs in scope.

options.text: Full user accounts with teams, billing and roles
options.why: A product on its own. Park it unless the interviewer asks.

options.text: A real-time analytics dashboard with charts by country and device
options.why: Out of scope here. A simple click count is enough. Name it as a future extension.

steps.explain: A strong opening is: **create**, **redirect**, **optional custom alias**, **optional expiry**. Say what you leave out (accounts, rich analytics) so the interviewer can correct you in the first five minutes instead of the last five.

notes: Core: create a short link, redirect, optional custom alias, optional expiry
Out of scope: user accounts, rich analytics

steps.title: How well must it work?
steps.prompt: Now the non-functional requirements. Which qualities does a URL shortener really need? Select all that apply.
steps.hint: Think about what a user feels. A slow or broken redirect is noticed by everyone who clicks the link.

options.text: Very high availability for redirects
options.why: If redirects fail, every link ever shared is broken, including links printed on paper.

options.text: Low redirect latency (tens of milliseconds on the server)
options.why: A redirect sits in front of the page the user wants, so any delay is added to every click.

options.text: Durability: a created link must never be lost
options.why: Losing a mapping breaks a link permanently.

options.text: Short codes should be hard to guess
options.why: Sequential codes let anyone enumerate other people's links.

options.text: Strong consistency for every read, everywhere, at all times
options.why: Costly and not needed. A link that appears a second or two late in another region is acceptable, and availability matters more.

options.text: Transactions across several tables on every request
options.why: The data is one key mapped to one value. There is nothing to join.

steps.explain: Redirects must be **fast and always up**. Creation can be a little slower. Because a lookup is by key, we can choose **availability over strict consistency** for reads. Say this explicitly.

notes: Redirects: highly available and fast
Mappings must be durable
Codes are not guessable
Eventual consistency is acceptable for reads

steps.title: How many links are created per second?
steps.prompt: Given **100 million** new links per month, what is the average number of **writes per second**? A rough number is enough.
steps.hint: A month has about 2.5 million seconds (30 days x 86,400).
steps.explain: **40 writes per second** is tiny. One ordinary database could handle it. So writes will not force a complicated design. The difficulty is elsewhere.

notes: Writes: about 40 per second on average

steps.title: And how many redirects per second?
steps.prompt: Reads are about **100 times** more common than writes. What is the average number of **redirects per second**?
work: Read : write = 100 : 1, so 40 x 100 = **4,000 reads per second**
Peak is usually 2 to 3 times the average, so plan for about **10,000 per second**
steps.explain: **4,000 average, around 10,000 at peak** is the number that shapes the design. A single database can struggle with this, and the same popular links are read again and again. That points to **caching** and a **read-optimised** design.

notes: Reads: about 4,000/s average, about 10,000/s peak (100:1 read-heavy)

steps.title: How much data over five years?
steps.prompt: Each record is about **500 bytes** and we keep links for **5 years**. How much storage do we need in total, in **terabytes**?
steps.hint: First count the records: links per month x 12 months x 5 years.
steps.explain: **About 3 TB** (plus replicas and indexes) is more than we would like on a single small machine, but it is not huge. It tells us we will **partition** the data eventually and that we should pick a store that scales horizontally.

notes: Storage: about 6 billion records, about 3 TB over 5 years

steps.title: How long must a short code be?
steps.prompt: Short codes use letters and digits: `a-z`, `A-Z`, `0-9` (**62** symbols, called base62). We need unique codes for **6 billion** links. What is the **minimum** length that works?
steps.hint: Compute 62 to the power 5, then 62 to the power 6, and compare with 6 billion.

options.text: 5 characters
options.why: 62^5 is about 916 million. That is less than 6 billion.

options.text: 6 characters
options.why: 62^6 is about 56.8 billion, enough for 6 billion links.

options.text: 7 characters
options.why: 62^7 is about 3.5 trillion. It works, but it is more than the minimum.

options.text: 10 characters
options.why: Plenty, but it makes the short link longer than it needs to be.

steps.explain: **6 characters** is the minimum (56.8 billion combinations). Many designs use **7** (3.5 trillion) for headroom, which also makes the codes harder to guess and leaves room for custom aliases. Either answer is fine if you explain it.

notes: Short code: base62, 7 characters (3.5 trillion combinations, about 6 billion needed)

steps.title: Which API fits?
steps.prompt: You define the public API. Which design is the best fit?
steps.hint: Creating something is a POST that returns a new resource. Opening a short link is a plain GET that answers with a redirect.

options.text: `POST /api/v1/urls` with `{long_url, alias?, expires_at?}` returns `201 {short_url}`, and `GET /{code}` returns a redirect
options.why: Clear separation. Creation is an API call. Redirect uses the short path itself so the link stays short.

options.text: `GET /create?url=...` to create and `GET /get?code=...` to redirect
options.why: Creating data with a GET is unsafe: browsers and crawlers can repeat it. The redirect path would also be long.

options.text: `POST /{code}` to redirect, with the code in the body
options.why: Browsers follow links with GET. A POST cannot be opened by clicking a link.

options.text: `PUT /api/v1/urls/{long_url}` to create, and `GET /api/v1/urls/{code}` to redirect
options.why: A long URL inside a URL path is awkward to encode, and the redirect path is longer than it should be.

steps.explain: Two endpoints are enough. `POST /api/v1/urls` takes the long URL (and optional alias and expiry) and returns the short URL. `GET /{code}` looks up the code and answers with a redirect. Mention an **API key and rate limit** on creation so the service cannot be flooded.

notes: API: POST /api/v1/urls -> 201 {short_url}; GET /{code} -> redirect

chapter.title: APIs, data model and choosing a database

steps.title: 301 or 302?
steps.prompt: The redirect can answer with **301 (permanent)** or **302 (temporary)**. Browsers cache a 301 and may never ask us again. Which should we use if we want click counts and expiring links to keep working?
steps.hint: Which one makes the browser come back to our server next time?

options.text: 301, because it is faster for the user
options.why: It is faster, but after the first visit the browser skips our server, so we cannot count clicks or enforce expiry.

options.text: 302, because every click still reaches our server
options.why: We can count the click, check expiry and even change the target later.

options.text: Either one, there is no difference
options.why: There is a big difference in caching behaviour.

steps.explain: Use **302** when you need analytics, expiry or the ability to edit a link. Use **301** when links never change and you want to save server load. This is a trade-off worth saying out loud.

notes: Redirect with 302 so clicks, expiry and edits keep working (cost: more traffic reaches us)

steps.title: Which kind of database?
steps.prompt: The data is `short_code -> long_url (+ created_at, expires_at, owner)`. The main query is: *give me the row for this code*. There are no joins. We expect billions of rows. What is the best fit?
steps.hint: Match the access pattern: single-key lookup, huge volume, no relationships.

options.text: A key-value or wide-column store keyed by short code
options.why: Single-key lookups, horizontal scaling and simple replication are exactly what these stores do best.

options.text: A single relational database with several normalised tables
options.why: It works at small scale, but one machine becomes the limit, and we would not use joins or multi-table transactions anyway.

options.text: A graph database
options.why: There are no relationships between links to traverse.

options.text: A search engine such as Elasticsearch
options.why: Great for text search, but we only need exact key lookup.

steps.explain: Choose a **key-value / wide-column store** (DynamoDB, Cassandra or similar), partitioned by `short_code`. A sharded relational database is also defensible if you explain how you would shard it. The point is to **tie the choice to the access pattern**.

notes: Store: key-value / wide-column, key = short_code
Record: short_code, long_url, created_at, expires_at, owner_id

chapter.title: APIs, data model and choosing a database

steps.title: Build the first version
steps.prompt: Time to put a first working design on the board. Which components belong on the path of a redirect request in version 1? Select all that apply.
steps.hint: Start simple: client, then whatever spreads traffic, then the servers, then the data. Add one thing that helps the read-heavy load.

options.text: Load balancer
options.why: Spreads requests across servers and removes a single server as a point of failure.

options.text: Stateless application servers
options.why: Any server can answer any request, so we can add more when traffic grows.

options.text: A cache in front of the database
options.why: 10,000 reads per second, mostly for the same popular links. A cache absorbs most of them.

options.text: The key-value database
options.why: The source of truth for every mapping.

options.text: A message queue between the user and the app server
options.why: A redirect must answer immediately. A queue adds delay and is not needed on this path.

options.text: A separate microservice for every endpoint
options.why: Do not open with microservices. Two endpoints do not need that complexity.

steps.explain: Version 1: **Client -> Load balancer -> App servers -> Cache -> Database**. Walk one request through: the app checks the cache; on a miss it reads the database, fills the cache and answers with a 302. Walk through a create request too.

notes: Redirect path: client -> load balancer -> app server -> cache -> database

steps.title: How do we create unique short codes?
steps.prompt: This is the heart of the problem. Many app servers create links at the same time, and **no two links may get the same code**. Which approach is the strongest?
steps.hint: Think about collisions, coordination between servers, and how each option behaves with many servers writing at once.

options.text: Hash the long URL (for example MD5) and keep the first 7 characters
options.why: Cutting a hash makes collisions likely, so you must check and retry on every write. The same URL always produces the same code, which is bad for per-user links.

options.text: Generate a random 7-character code and retry if it already exists
options.why: Simple, but every write needs a database check, and as the table fills, retries grow.

options.text: A counter converted to base62, where each server takes a block of numbers (for example 1 million at a time) from a coordinator
options.why: No collisions by construction, no per-write database check, and servers only talk to the coordinator once per block.

options.text: Use the database auto-increment ID of one primary database for everything
options.why: Correct but it makes one database the bottleneck and a single point of failure for all writes.

steps.explain: **Counter ranges + base62** wins: each server asks a small coordinator (ZooKeeper, etcd or a tiny database table) for a range, then hands out numbers locally and converts them with base62. Collisions cannot happen. Cost: if a server crashes you lose the unused part of its block, which is harmless with 3.5 trillion codes.

notes: IDs: counter ranges from a coordinator, converted to base62; no collisions, no per-write lookup

steps.title: Counters are guessable. Fix it.
steps.prompt: A counter gives codes like `aaaaab`, `aaaaac`, `aaaaad`. Someone can walk through them and read other people's links. **Write down** how you would keep the benefits of the counter but make the codes hard to guess.
steps.hint: You do not have to change the counter. Change what the user sees.
points: Scramble the counter number with a reversible mixing step (for example XOR with a secret, bit shuffling or a Feistel network) before base62 encoding
Still unique, because a reversible mix never maps two numbers to the same output
Alternative: a key generation service that pre-creates random unused codes and hands them out
Optional: make private links use a longer code
steps.model: Keep the counter, but pass the number through a **reversible scramble** (a Feistel network, or multiply by a large number coprime with the range, modulo the size of the code space) before encoding as base62. Because the scramble is a one-to-one mapping, uniqueness is preserved, yet consecutive numbers produce codes that look random. Another option is a **key generation service** that pre-fills a table with random unused codes. It is easy to reason about but needs a place to store and mark codes as used.
steps.explain: Uniqueness and unpredictability are two different problems. Solve uniqueness with the counter, then solve unpredictability with a reversible scramble.

notes: Scramble the counter value (reversible, so still unique) before base62 so codes are not guessable

steps.title: How big does the cache need to be?
steps.prompt: Reads are about 4,000 per second. A small share of links (about **20%**) gets most of the traffic. If we cache the **hot 20% of one day's reads** at 500 bytes each, how much memory do we need, in **GB**?
steps.hint: Reads per day = 4,000 x 86,400. Then take 20% and multiply by 500 bytes.
work: 20% of that = about 69 million cache entries
steps.explain: **About 35 GB** fits in the memory of a single large cache machine, and certainly in a small cluster. That means caching the hot links is cheap and absorbs most of the 10,000 reads per second. Use **cache-aside** with **LRU** eviction, and a **TTL** that never outlives the link's expiry.

notes: Cache: cache-aside, LRU eviction, about 35 GB for the hot 20%

steps.title: Choose the shard key
steps.prompt: 3 TB will not live happily on one machine, so we **shard** (split) the data. What should the shard key be?
steps.hint: Which key do we always have when we serve a read? And which choice spreads traffic evenly?

options.text: A hash of the short code
options.why: Every redirect knows the code, so it goes to exactly one shard. Hashing spreads data and traffic evenly.

options.text: The user who created the link
options.why: A redirect request does not know the owner. One heavy user would also create a hot shard.

options.text: The creation date
options.why: All new writes hit the newest shard, and recent links get the most reads. That creates a hot spot.

options.text: The first letter of the code
options.why: Uneven distribution and only 62 shards at most. Hash instead.

steps.explain: Shard by **hash(short_code)**, ideally with **consistent hashing** so that adding a shard moves only a small share of the data. Keep **replicas** of each shard for durability and for spreading reads.

notes: Shard by hash(short_code) with consistent hashing; replicate each shard

steps.title: What can fail, and what do we do?
steps.prompt: Walk the design looking for weak points. Which of these are **good** measures? Select all that apply.
steps.hint: For each box on the diagram ask: if this dies, what happens to a redirect?

options.text: Run several load balancers and app servers across availability zones
options.why: Removes single points of failure in the stateless layers.

options.text: Replicate each shard across zones with automatic failover
options.why: A lost machine or zone must not lose data or stop reads.

options.text: If the cache fails, fall back to the database but limit the load with request coalescing and rate limits
options.why: All traffic suddenly hitting the database is a classic cascade. Protect it.

options.text: Rate limit link creation per user or IP, and put timeouts and retries with backoff on every call
options.why: Stops abuse and keeps a slow dependency from tying up every thread.

options.text: Run the counter coordinator as a single instance to keep it simple
options.why: A single coordinator is a single point of failure for writes. Run it as a small replicated cluster.

options.text: Back up the data once a year
options.why: Far too rare. Use continuous replication plus regular snapshots and test the restore.

steps.explain: Remove every single point of failure, plan what happens when each box dies, and **protect the database from a cache outage**. Add **monitoring and alerts** on redirect latency, error rate, cache hit rate and replication lag.

notes: Redundancy in every layer across zones
Cache outage: fall back to DB with request coalescing and rate limits
Monitor latency, errors, cache hit rate and replication lag

steps.title: Defend your design
steps.prompt: The interviewer asks: *"What did you give up with this design, and what would make you change it?"* **Write** two or three trade-offs in your own words before you look at the model answer.
steps.hint: Use the pattern: I chose X, which costs Y. If Z changed, I would revisit it.
points: 302 redirects keep analytics and expiry working but send more traffic to our servers
Eventual consistency and caching mean a new or changed link may be briefly stale
Counter ranges waste a few numbers when a server crashes, which is harmless
A key-value store gives up joins and flexible queries, so rich analytics would need a separate pipeline
If the product needed accounts, editing and reports, I would revisit the storage choice
steps.model: I chose a **302** so clicks, expiry and edits keep working. The cost is more traffic hitting our servers than a 301 would cause. I chose **eventual consistency and caching** for reads to keep redirects fast and available. The cost is that an updated or deleted link may be served stale for a short time (bounded by the cache TTL). **Counter ranges** guarantee unique codes without a lookup per write; the cost is that numbers are wasted when a server dies, which does not matter with trillions available. A **key-value store** scales easily for our single access pattern, but I give up joins, so rich analytics would go to a separate event pipeline (a queue feeding a columnar store). If requirements grew to accounts and reporting, I would revisit this.
steps.explain: Strong answers do not claim a choice is obviously correct. They name the cost and the trigger that would change the decision.

notes: Trade-offs named: 302 vs traffic, eventual consistency vs latency, KV store vs flexible queries
